summary: Specifies a mechanism for a DNSSEC validating resolver to signal which trust anchors it has loaded, so that others can tell if it is ready for a root key rollover. The check works through special names in DNS queries.

eli5.summary: Before changing a lock, you test who has the new key. This lets you check which resolvers are ready.

questions: what is the dnssec root key sentinel
how to test if a resolver has the new root ksk
what is a key tag in dnssec
subtitle: Special DNS names let anyone test whether a validating resolver already trusts a new root key.

tldr.problem: Before the root zone Key Signing Key (KSK) is replaced, users and researchers want to know whether the resolvers they depend on have loaded the new key. A resolver without it would stop validating and users would lose DNS service.
tldr.mechanism: Validating resolvers recognise two special leftmost labels, root-key-sentinel-is-ta- and root-key-sentinel-not-ta- followed by a Key Tag. Depending on whether that key is in the trust-anchor store, the resolver returns the normal answer or SERVFAIL, and the pattern of answers reveals the key state.
tldr.outcome: A client that queries three names can tell whether it will be affected by a KSK roll. The mechanism is OPTIONAL to implement, and it only reports on root keys.

today: RFC 8509 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the sentinel mechanism for root keys only.

sections.title: Why a Key Sentinel Is Needed
sections.content:
DNSSEC uses digital signatures to protect DNS data, and validating resolvers check those signatures starting from a trust anchor. A DNSKEY record has a 16-bit Key Tag, and RRSIG records carry the Key Tag of the key that made the signature.

This RFC specifies how a validating resolver can answer certain queries so that the asker can deduce whether a particular root key is in the resolver's trusted-key store. The tests can show whether a root zone Key Signing Key (KSK) is ready to be trusted, in the context of a planned root KSK roll.

There are two main use cases: users who want to know whether their resolver is ready for a rollover, and researchers who want Internet-wide measurements of how many users a rollover would hurt. The mechanism is OPTIONAL to implement, but if it is implemented it SHOULD be enabled by default to help measurement, and it MAY be disabled by local policy.

The RFC notes that this differs from RFC 8145, where resolvers report their cached root trust anchors to the root servers. Those reports help estimate how many resolvers are affected, but not what the user impact will be.
sections.eli5: Imagine the town is about to swap a lock and you want to know if your house has the new key. This is a way to find out before the swap happens.

sections.title: The Two Special Labels
sections.content:
The mechanism uses two special leftmost labels in a query name: root-key-sentinel-is-ta-<key-tag> and root-key-sentinel-not-ta-<key-tag>. The first asks, is this the Key Tag of a key the resolver currently trusts as a trust anchor? The second asks the opposite.

The <key-tag> is an unsigned decimal integer zero-padded to five digits, so a Key Tag of 42 appears as 00042. A label that is not zero-padded to five digits does not match and is handled like any other label.

The RFC says these labels were chosen after extensive IETF evaluation. Underscore-prefixed names were rejected because some browsers and operating systems would not fetch names that are not valid hostnames. It also warns that reserving leftmost labels this way is definitely not considered best practice.
sections.eli5: The special names are like secret passwords added to the front of a web address. A resolver that knows the trick treats them differently from normal names.

sections.title: When Special Processing Applies
sections.content:
A resolver only alters a response when every precondition holds: the response is DNSSEC validated, the result is Secure, the Checking Disabled (CD) bit is not set in the query, the QTYPE is A or AAAA (value 1 or 28), the OPCODE is QUERY, and the leftmost label of the original QNAME is one of the two sentinel labels. If any one fails, the resolver MUST NOT alter the response.

The resolver then checks whether the label's Key Tag matches an active root zone KSK in its trusted-key store. An active key is one that could currently be used for validation, meaning not in the AddPend or Revoked state of RFC 5011.

The outcome follows a small table. For is-ta, a trusted key gives the original answer and an untrusted key gives SERVFAIL. For not-ta it is reversed. "Return SERVFAIL" means RCODE 2 with an empty Answer Section.
sections.eli5: The resolver only plays the trick when everything checks out. Then it either hands over the real answer or says "something is wrong", depending on whether it has that key.

sections.title: Testing a Single Resolver
sections.content:
To test one recursive resolver, a client sends three queries: a name starting with the is-ta label, a name starting with the not-ta label (both under any validly signed zone), and a name whose DNSSEC signature cannot be validated, a "bogus" RRset. The test relies on validating resolvers returning SERVFAIL for the bogus name.

The responses sort resolvers into five types. Vnew has the nominated key and answers is-ta, fails not-ta and fails bogus. Vold implements the mechanism but lacks the key, so it fails is-ta, answers not-ta and fails bogus. Vind does not implement the mechanism, so it answers both sentinel names and fails bogus, which says nothing about its trust anchors. nonV does not validate and answers all three. other covers any other mix, for example a resolver farm whose members behave differently.

SERVFAIL might be cached for up to 5 minutes, and a positive answer for up to its TTL. Forwarders complicate matters. A validating resolver that sets the CD bit on all forwarded queries acts like a standalone resolver. If both resolvers support the mechanism, the CD bit is not set and their key states differ, the result is indeterminate (Vind) or mixed (other).
sections.eli5: You ask three questions and look at which ones get a real answer and which get an error. The pattern tells you whether the resolver has the key, does not have it, or cannot say.

sections.title: Testing a Set of Resolvers
sections.content:
Most users have more than one resolver configured, so the single-resolver test is unreliable: a SERVFAIL from one resolver may make the stub resolver retry another. The multi-resolver test is therefore narrower. It does not reveal the trust anchors of any one resolver. It targets a root KSK roll in which "KSK-current" will be replaced by "KSK-new", and it is designed to run after KSK-new is introduced into the root zone and before the zone is signed with it.

The goal is to find out whether the user will be negatively impacted, which happens when all configured resolvers validate and none has loaded KSK-new. The test assumes the stub resolver tries each configured resolver on SERVFAIL until it gets a non-SERVFAIL answer or runs out, that answers are consistent over the time of the queries, and that all validating resolvers have KSK-current. The RFC says no published measurement data shows how well the first two assumptions hold.

The three queries are the invalid name, not-ta with the Key Tag of KSK-current, and is-ta with the Key Tag of KSK-new. Results are written as triplets of S (SERVFAIL) or A (an answer), in that order.

  • (A * *): at least one resolver does not validate, so the user is not impacted.
  • (S A *): at least one resolver does not recognise the sentinel, so the outcome cannot be determined.
  • (S S A): all validate, all know the sentinel, and at least one has KSK-new, so the user is not impacted.
  • (S S S): all validate, all know the sentinel, and none has KSK-new, so the user will be negatively impacted.
sections.eli5: When you have several helpers, you ask all of them at once. If any one of them knows the new key, you are fine. If none do, you will lose service when the key changes.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The mechanism does not require resolvers to mark otherwise unauthenticated responses as authenticated, and it does not change how DNSSEC authenticity is interpreted. It needs no significant extra processing, and sentinel queries add no load beyond normal DNSSEC validation that an attacker could exploit.

The privacy section points out that if the user runs third-party code, that party may learn the information too. Someone who can make a user issue specific DNS queries, for example through web ads or JavaScript, can learn about the user's resolvers. With additional knowledge of which resolvers are used, they can determine which trust anchors those resolvers hold. Without it, they can only infer the aggregate capabilities of the user's DNS environment.

There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The trick does not make anything less safe, but a website you visit could use it to peek at how your resolvers are set up.

sections.title: Walk-Through Example
sections.content:
The appendix is a non-normative story. Alice wants to roll the root KSK from Key Tag 11112 to a new KSK with Key Tag 02323. Researcher Geoff publishes three AAAA records in a signed example.com zone: a deliberately bogus name, root-key-sentinel-is-ta-02323 and root-key-sentinel-not-ta-11112, and serves a small image for each from a web server.

Four users browse to the page. Bob's ISP does not validate, so he can fetch the bogus name and is fine. Charlie's resolvers validate but do not implement the sentinel, so he cannot fetch the bogus name but can fetch both others, and gets no definitive answer. Dave's resolvers have the new key, so he fetches the is-ta name but not the bogus or not-ta names, and will not be impacted. Ed's resolvers lack 02323, so he can fetch none of the three, and will be negatively impacted.

In practice, JavaScript would show the result, and the mechanism does not depend on the web: querying with a tool such as dig and checking which names return SERVFAIL works as well.
sections.eli5: Four friends test their internet helpers. Some pass, some cannot tell, and one finds out they will lose service unless their helper gets the new key.
